newsitem.title: USA: Lark campaign was invitation to lawsuits-documents.
newsitem.headline: Lark campaign was invitation to lawsuits-documents.

text.p: A Liggett Group attorney advised the cigarette company that a 1970s Lark-brand campaign was "an invitation to cancer litigation," according to company documents released on Monday.

In an April 7, 1975, legal memorandum to Liggett, attorney Joseph Greer said the planned advertising campaign "in effect was an admission against its interests that a person can 'enjoy smoking too much' and, in fact, can smoke too much."

Greer went on to advise that the proposed advertising campaign, which was to have included such slogans as "Because you enjoy smoking too much", was opening Liggett to potential legal problems and cautioned against positioning Lark as a safe cigarette.

Greer's memorandum and six other documents made public on Monday after a pre-trial hearing in Florida's Medicaid lawsuit against the tobacco industry are among the first public disclosures from papers Liggett has promised to deliver to anti-tobacco lawyers.

The Arizona Republic newspaper last week published excerpts from the documents quoting executives of Liggett, a unit of Brooke Group Ltd, as weighing a substitute for nicotine because of its "severe toxicity" and designing packaging to appeal to youths.

Other slogans and advertising headlines considered for the Lark campaign included: "The only real alternative for the heavy smoker", "The only alternative for the real smoker" and "For people who really love to smoke."
Greer also wrote that the advertising by implication suggested Lark was a "safer and healthier cigarette to smoke.
"This is a health claim, at least by implication, which may lead directly to litigation and possibly resultant liability," he added.

Tobacco company lawyers agreed to release seven of 20 documents, saying they were dropping claims of privilege since the seven were only about Liggett. The thirteen other documents are covered by attorney-client and trade-secret privileges, the tobacco lawyers said.
Florida state lawyers claim the remaining documents contain information regarding public safety and must be released under the states Sunshine Act.

Special Master William Rutter, appointed by trial judge Harold Cohen of Palm Beach County Court, is expected to rule on the remaining 13 documents and forward a recommendation to Cohen for an April 14 hearing.
Two of the seven documents refer to Liggett advertising matters, while the remainder dealt with cigarette additives and tobacco production details.

Although Liggett agreed to release the documents in March, as part of a settlement with 22 state attorneys general suing it and other tobacco companies, the papers have largely been seen only by judges.

A North Carolina state judge imposed a restraining order on March 20, but the order has been repeatedly ignored by judges in other states readying for tobacco trials in coming months. Florida is seeking $1 billion or more it spent treating sick smokers.
